prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 class of topological insulators, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B028 as my preferred single achievement. After the first round, four of us independently name the same three people, and nobody disputes that the effect is real or reproduced. The scientific core is a simple, general idea: spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry give a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states, first written down by Kane and Mele for graphene. Molenkamp's group then observed the edge channel transport in HgTe wells, and about two decades of independent work in 2D and 3D materials followed. This is the sort of case where calculation, spectra and transport agree, and that is the test I apply first. I now regard the citation as the key decision. If it is built on the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and on the first observation of the quantum spin Hall state, then every name in it can defend their part of it. Pearce proposed exactly this narrowing, and I agree with him. As to the chair's question about 2016: the 2016 prize rewarded topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter in model systems (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz). B028 is about symmetry-protected band topology in real spin-orbit-coupled materials, a class that can be identified from band structure, and that is a different and later achievement.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary remains the real weakness and I do not think the round-1 exchange removed it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe quantum well realisation that Molenkamp tested, and they are not in the credited names. Hasan's ARPES work on Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3, together with Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents and Roy, is the 3D strand and is left out of a trio of this kind. The HgTe edge conductance was well short of perfect quantisation, so a sceptic can call the experimental half thin, as Mehlig says. A prize two years after a topological prize can also look like a repeat to outside readers, and practical applications are still modest. I accept these costs. Choosing between them and the alternatives, I find the credit cost of B028 more tolerable than the maturity cost of B046, and more tolerable than the incremental-precision question that hangs over B034.

responses.point: Danielsson asks whether B028 is as new as it feels two years after the 2016 prize, says the trio is easier to get wrong because Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan are live claims, and keeps B005 plus a MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero part as his configuration.
responses.response: I have tried to answer the 2016 question directly, because it is a fair one. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and topological quantum matter in idealised models. Kane and Mele predicted a concrete, spin-orbit-driven Z2 state in a real band structure, and Molenkamp measured it. That sequence is the origin of the whole materials class, so I do not think the two prizes overlap. On credit, I agree it is not unique and I accept that. But I would point out that all three of your candidate parts have a credit problem too: you concede this for IceCube and for the two-name moire part. On the two-part idea: I do not support it, because I cannot judge the neutrino case, and I am wary of a prize that pairs a detector collaboration with a single name. I would be glad to know whether you can defend Halzen alone against AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal. If you can't, your own statement says you would not oppose B028, and I would welcome that.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B046 alone with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer, argues an unexplained mechanism should not delay a prize (the cuprates were honoured before they were understood), and moved from Andrei to Bistritzer.
responses.response: Your cuprate comparison is a good one and it has moved me part of the way. I no longer treat the open pairing mechanism as disqualifying, and I have kept B046 as my first alternative. I still weigh two things differently. First, the cuprates were recognised after a decade with broad materials-level confirmation, and the moire phases are still sensitive to sample, twist angle and disorder; I would like a bit more time to see which phases survive across devices and which are fragile. Second, your move to Bistritzer is correct in my view because the 2011 model has two authors, but it does leave Andrei and the earlier continuum-model theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) unresolved, and that credit story is less settled than the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp one. If the committee tilts to B046, I could support the Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer slate. For now I think it is a year or two less settled than B028.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, would word the citation around the 2D quantum spin Hall prediction and first observation, and asks whether the committee should accept a trio that omits Hasan or handle the 3D strand with a second part.
responses.response: I agree with your narrowing and I have adopted it in my citation. To your direct question: I would accept a trio that omits Hasan, and I would not add a second part. A second part would take the third name or force a fourth, which the three-person cap forbids, and Mehlig's proposal to swap Hasan for Mele or Molenkamp would remove one of the two people who define the central idea or the first experiment. The Z2 classification of Kane and Mele is what unifies the 2D and 3D cases, so the citation can name the Z2 class of topological insulators without claiming the 3D ARPES discovery. I acknowledge that Hasan and the BHZ theorists may read this as an omission. I think it is an honest one provided that the words of the citation do not claim more than the three names did.

responses.point: Mehlig says a slate with Hasan would be at least as defensible, that the HgTe edge conductance fell short of perfect quantisation, and that the citation should be narrow enough to avoid misstating history.
responses.response: I agree with the last point and have written the citation accordingly: it speaks of prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 class, and of the first observation in HgTe, and it does not say who discovered 3D topological insulators. On Hasan I still differ with you. A slate that replaces Molenkamp with Hasan loses the experimental test of the very Z2 mechanism, and a slate that replaces Mele loses half the theory. You are right that the quantisation in HgTe was imperfect, but the nonlocal and edge transport results have been repeated, and for me this is a normal level of imperfection for a first observation of a mesoscopic effect. I take the point that the experimental half is thinner than the theory, and it is the reason my confidence in B028 is high but not overwhelming.

responses.point: Kroll prefers optical lattice clocks (Katori and Ye) for their clean two-name credit, their reproduction in several laboratories and new observables such as millimetre-scale redshift and searches for varying constants.
responses.response: I gave B034 as my second alternative for exactly the reasons you mention: the attribution is cleaner than anything in condensed matter and the reproduction is excellent. You asked yourself what the discovery is beyond capability, and in my view that is still open. The redshift over millimetres is a real result, but it confirms general relativity, and the searches for constants and dark matter have so far produced limits. I would put this as a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 lines of work, however impressive. I would not oppose a clocks prize, and I would call it the safest result if the topological credit cannot be settled, but I would be giving up a discovery of a new class of matter for it.

uncertainties: Whether the narrow citation (prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, plus the first HgTe observation) will be read by the community as a fair statement of history given the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan.
Whether B046 is better preferred if the committee judges its breadth to outweigh the unsettled pairing mechanism; I would accept it with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer.
I rely on memory for priority and chronology details and have not verified them independently; I defer on IceCube and on the physics of optical clocks.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no collaboration with any credited name on the shortlist and no institutional tie to any candidate. As a theorist who computes band structures I may favour candidates where theory and spectra agree, and I flag that this tilts me toward B028. I do not think recusal is needed.
